data.title: Oracle Stock Is a Waiting Game, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has become one of the more divisive stocks in the AI trade. The longtime database company has turned itself into a major supplier of computing power for AI developers, but its shares sit 59% below their highs as investors question how much it is spending to build data centers.

The question now is whether the lower share price is a buying opportunity or a sign that the stock has lost its luster.

One investor who sees room for the shares to climb is John Ballard, who contributes to The Motley Fool. Ballard, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, believes Oracle’s huge order book could more than double the stock by 2029, as long as a few things go right.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

Ballard’s case is built on remaining performance obligations (RPO), which are signed contracts that have not yet been booked as revenue. RPO reached $664 billion in Oracle’s fiscal first quarter (August quarter). That is $209 billion more than a year earlier and $26 billion more than the prior quarter. Management expects about half of it to turn into sales within three years. Because the money is already under contract, Ballard sees it as a fairly reliable guide to future revenue, especially while the industry still cannot build AI capacity fast enough.

Recent results support that view. Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% year over year to $7.4 billion. GPU utilization was 97.9%, and capacity that came up for renewal was re-signed or resold at a 20% premium. For fiscal 2027, Oracle is guiding for at least $90 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of $8.10. Ballard also points to industry data. Synergy Research Group found that generative AI cloud services grew 165%, with Oracle among the fastest growers outside the big three. Goldman Sachs expects the five largest U.S. hyperscalers to spend about $1.2 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2027.

On valuation, the stock trades at about 20 times earnings. Wall Street’s average estimate for fiscal 2029 EPS is $15.80. If Oracle hits that number and keeps the same multiple, the shares would land near $316, almost 140% above the current price.

The 5-star investor is open about why the multiple is low. Oracle plans $90 billion to $95 billion in capital spending this fiscal year. Customer prepayments and similar deals should bring the net cash outlay down to $70 billion or less. Even so, free cash flow was negative $5 billion last quarter. A large share of the backlog also comes from a handful of customers. Any delay in getting data centers running could slow how quickly the backlog becomes revenue and leave earnings short of forecasts.

Nevertheless, Ballard argues that accelerating infrastructure growth, nearly full GPU usage, and the ability to raise prices on renewals make a believable bull case, provided Oracle builds on schedule. (To watch Ballard’s track record, click here)

Most of the analyst community takes a similar stance. Based on a mix of 27 Buys, 5 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock receives a Strong Buy consensus rating. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 89%, given the average target clocks in at $245.39. (See Oracle stock forecast)

data.title: CoreWeave vs. IREN: One AI Stock to Avoid, One to Embrace, Says Investor
data.description:
CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) and IREN (NASDAQ:IREN) are both under pressure today, as the market grows jittery about the rising borrowing costs facing AI cloud providers. The pullback adds to recent losses, leaving both stocks down more than 50% over the past year.

The two companies are in the same business. Both rent GPU computing power to AI developers, and both are spending heavily on data centers to keep up with demand. The difference is who pays for the buildout. CoreWeave relies mostly on debt and equity markets, and those markets have turned on the stock in recent weeks. IREN has convinced customers to pay for a large part of its hardware upfront.

That gap is the focus of a recent comparison by an investor using the moniker Infinity Curve (IC), who has been taking a look at both stocks. The investor keeps coming back to one question: once the chips are bought and the lenders are paid, how much is actually left for shareholders?

Promotion

High conviction CRWV bulls now have this Tradr ETF

With CoreWeave, IC’s concern starts with the bond market. CRWV shares have been hammered over the past week, while the company’s five-year credit default swaps moved past 1,000 basis points, and its unsecured notes due 2031 fell far enough to yield close to 15%. IC notes that none of this means the company has missed a payment or broken a covenant. But for a business that depends on outside money to grow, a sharp jump in funding costs is hard to wave away.

The balance sheet shows why. At the end of June, CoreWeave carried about $35.6 billion in debt principal and $16.3 billion in operating lease liabilities, compared with $5.5 billion in unrestricted cash. Its free cash flow deficit grew from roughly $4.7 billion in Q1 to $5.7 billion in Q2.

The two pressures also reinforce each other. A September agreement lets CoreWeave sell up to 35 million shares. At the October 7 price, that block was worth about $3.1 billion. After the selloff, it was worth roughly $2.4 billion. Expensive debt makes selling stock more attractive, but a lower stock price means more dilution for every dollar raised.

On the other hand, the investor doesn’t see a demand problem. Nothing suggests customers are walking away, and the company guided Q3 revenue to $3.45 billion to $3.60 billion. What matters to IC is whether new capacity brings in more cash on its own, rather than needing more corporate debt or new shares to fund it.

At around 1.6x consensus 2027 sales, the stock looks cheap for a company expected to more than double revenue. The investor argues, though, that a sales multiple ignores debt, leases, and the cost of replacing GPUs. As such, IC takes a bearish view here now. “I sold my CRWV shares a few days ago, and for now, I am staying on the sidelines until I see clearer confirmation that financing conditions are stabilizing,” IC summed up, rating the stock a Sell. (To watch Infinity Curve’s track record, click here)

IREN looks different to the investor because of how its assets age. GPUs need replacing every few years, but power connections, cooling systems and buildings can serve several generations of chips. Recent IREN customers have prepaid 45% to 55% of GPU costs, and lenders have covered up to about 90% of GPU spending on some deployments. With contracts bringing in more than $20 million per megawatt each year, management estimates the GPUs can pay for themselves in about two years. In effect, the first customer helps pay for infrastructure that will outlast its contract.

That’s where IC sees the real upside. The next deployment starts with a site that’s already partly paid for, so most new spending goes to chips rather than rebuilding everything. Each successful contract leaves IREN in a stronger position for the next one, and over time that could push returns well above what today’s financial statements show. Management also says older GPUs can keep earning after their five-year depreciation period by moving from AI training to simpler inference work, which would improve the economics further.

The investor’s main caveat is about cash. Most of IREN’s operating cash flow in the June quarter came from customer prepayments for services not yet delivered, and collecting cash early isn’t the same as generating free cash. The figure to watch is cash per megawatt after debt payments, maintenance and reserves.

On valuation, IREN trades at 5.64x forward EV/sales, below peers MARA at 8.30x and RIOT at 9.97x, two bitcoin miners also moving into AI infrastructure. Its expected revenue growth of about 143% is the highest in that group. It also trades at 8.43x forward EBITDA, with EBITDA growth projected at around 178%. With $4 billion in contracted annual revenue and plenty of capacity still to develop, IC thinks the market hasn’t caught up to the AI buildout. “I continue to be bullish on IREN as the upside story goes beyond the first GPU cycle,” IC wrapped up. “If the cost of computing is recovered by the customers in their funded deployments while the renewable energy and data center structure is left behind, profits will continue to get better with each cycle.”

As such, Infinity Curve rates IREN stock a Buy.

On the Street, both stocks receive Moderate Buy consensus ratings and are projected to generate big gains. CRWV’s $143.59 average price target points to 12-month returns of 126%. Meanwhile, IREN is expected to gain an even more impressive 183%, given the average target lands at $79.30. (See CRWV stock forecast or IREN stock forecast)

data.title: ‘A Nothingburger,’ Says Investor About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) investors really did not appreciate the space company’s latest update and headed to the exit gate in droves on Thursday, after the company said the first flight of its Neutron rocket will slip into 2027 and miss its earlier fourth-quarter 2026 target.

Neutron forms a big part of the Rocket Lab bull case because it can carry far heavier payloads than the company’s smaller Electron rocket, which would let Rocket Lab pursue larger commercial and government missions and compete more directly with SpaceX. Investors had been counting on a year-end launch to lift the stock, after it had already endured a massive pullback from May’s high.

But as any savvy investor knows, the market sometimes has a tendency to overreact to bad news, and in this case, investor Amrita Roy believes that is the case. In fact, Roy calls the selloff a gift, as she thinks the market is overlooking the bigger picture.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

CEO Peter Beck explained that inspectors found voids, which are tiny air pockets, between the carbon fiber layers of a forward propellant tank dome on the rocket’s first stage. These gaps can weaken the part. This is Neutron’s second manufacturing setback, following an earlier tank issue that pushed Rocket Lab toward automated production.

Rocket Lab hasn’t set a new launch date yet. Beck said the replacement dome should be built and inspected before the first quarter of 2027, with tank assembly and testing during that quarter, and only then will the company name a target. Engineers were able to recreate the defect and adjust the process, which Roy sees as a sign of a fixable production issue rather than a deeper engineering problem. Rocket Lab is also using the extra time to bring forward upgrades meant for later flights, with the second and third rockets already in production. Beck also expects more Neutron contracts to be announced.

Meanwhile, the rest of the company is doing well. Second-quarter revenue reached a record $234.1 million, up 62% year-over-year, while the backlog hit about $2.36 billion, with nearly half expected to turn into revenue within a year. Since Space Systems brings in over 80% of sales, Roy sees a solid cushion while Neutron catches up.

The upcoming Iridium deal adds to the appeal. Iridium shareholders approved the acquisition in September, and once regulators sign off, Rocket Lab will gain a 66-satellite constellation and valuable L-band spectrum. Roy believes this brings the company closer to controlling everything from building satellites to selling services, a model only SpaceX has so far.

All of that makes RKLB a Buy to Roy, although the investor is only making it a small position, given the “volatile nature of the company.” (To watch Roy’s track record, click here)

Most of the Street’s analysts also see the stock as a sound choice. Based on 15 Buys vs. 3 Holds, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. Meanwhile, the $100.25 average price target points to 12-month returns of 87%. (See RKLB stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Don’t Let the Run Fool You,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock has been under pressure this week as fears over competition from Chinese memory maker CXMT have caused havoc in the memory segment. The stock was already struggling to gain traction after its latest blockbuster earnings report, as worries about how long the AI spending spree can last, along with the memory market’s history of boom-and-bust cycles, have kept investors cautious.

Zoom out, though, and the picture looks very different. The stock is still up roughly 207% so far in 2026, making it one of the S&P 500’s top performers.

Now, usually when a stock has surged like that, investors would be wary of wading in. However, top investor Keithen Drury, who contributes to The Motley Fool, believes the story still has plenty of room to run.

Promotion

Discover why XOVR identified Kalshi as an attractive private investment opportunity.

Drury’s case rests on the idea that Micron is breaking away from the patterns that have long made it a tricky stock to own. Memory chips are largely interchangeable, so manufacturers have little control over pricing. When demand is strong, everyone wins. When supply catches up, companies are stuck with unsold inventory, and their shares take the hit.

At the moment, the AI infrastructure boom has led to the strongest memory demand cycle on record. DRAM and NAND supply is fully booked, sending prices sharply higher. The big question is what happens when that demand cools.

This is where Drury sees real change. Micron has signed multi-year take-or-pay agreements with customers, most of which include minimum and maximum prices. The company estimates these deals will account for more than 35% of its revenue through 2030. “That’s a huge step toward ending the cyclicality of Micron’s business, as Micron is now being treated more like a true supplier rather than just a commodity dealer,” Drury, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, said.

The investor also highlights a first-of-its-kind custom high-bandwidth memory product Micron is developing with Nvidia for its GPUs, which could change how Micron works with a key customer.

As for timing, many investors expect AI spending to ease around 2030. However, Micron recently said some customer agreements now run to 2031. Management also expects supply to be even tighter in 2027 and 2028 than this year, as significant new capacity won’t come online until the middle of next year at the earliest. For Drury, that suggests the company’s sales have room to keep climbing for some time.

All of this has convinced Drury to open a position. The 5-star investor thinks Micron should trade more like a big tech name until at least 2030 and expects the shares to deliver solid returns. Still, Drury plans to watch the memory market carefully and will change his stance if conditions start to sour. (To watch Drury’s track record, click here)

Almost all of the Street’s analysts concur. Based on 27 Buys vs. 1 Hold, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Going by the $1,621.67 average price target, a year from now, shares will be changing hands for an 80% premium. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: ‘A Flying Car Doesn’t Change the Math,’ Says Top Investor About Tesla Stock
data.description:
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) shares are climbing today in premarket trading after the company finally showed off its long-delayed second-generation Roadster. At a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday night, the car flipped in midair, drove upside down along a curved ramp, and set down using cold-gas thrusters supplied by Elon Musk’s rocket company. Tesla claimed a 0-60 mph time of 0.81 seconds and said production should start in 2028.

The bounce is welcome for a stock that is still down about 19% this year, and the timing matters, with third-quarter results due on October 21.

But not everyone is impressed. 5-star investor Julia Ostian, who wrote ahead of the reveal, argues that a great show doesn’t fix what’s underneath.

Promotion

Explore TSLQ for 2X short leverage on TSLA

Ostian saw the event as a sentiment play from the start. The Roadster was first unveiled in 2017 with a 2020 production target, and Tesla’s own Q2 materials still listed it as in design development with no factory assigned. Even if it eventually ships, it will be a niche, low-volume car with little impact on revenue or profits.

The bigger worry is profitability. Second-quarter sales grew 26% year-over-year to $28.24 billion, but operating margin shrank to just 1.4%, leaving Tesla with roughly a penny and a half of operating profit on each dollar of sales. Automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits slipped to 16.3%, and energy margins roughly halved after a warranty charge. Ostian also notes that about $1 billion of GAAP net income came from a paper gain on Tesla’s SpaceX stake. Strip that out, and adjusted EPS of $0.33 fell about 25% short of forecasts.

Cash is another sore spot. Capital spending more than doubled to $5.79 billion, pushing free cash flow to about negative $1.1 billion. Management expects capex above $25 billion this year and has arranged debt facilities of up to $30 billion. In Ostian’s view, shareholders are bankrolling a massive bet, including a chip venture with SpaceX, while the core business doesn’t earn enough to justify it.

Ostian, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, does acknowledge some bright spots. Third-quarter deliveries of 486,532 vehicles beat expectations by about 5%, and FSD subscriptions jumped 56% to 1.48 million. However, Tesla delivered around 22,000 more cars than it built, and with discounts running in China, Ostian expects selling prices to remain under pressure.

Then there’s valuation. Tesla trades at about 215 times forward non-GAAP earnings, compared with a sector median near 15x, and carries a forward PEG ratio of 11.5, against 1.25 for the sector. Even using 2027 estimates, the multiple sits around 174x. For Ostian, the stock is priced as if robots, robotaxis, and chips have already delivered, and a flying car doesn’t change that math.

Accordingly, Ostian rates Tesla stock a Strong Sell. (To watch Ostian’s track record, click here)

On the Street, 2 analysts agree with that stance, but with an additional 14 Buys and 11 Holds, the stock receives a Moderate Buy consensus rating. Going by the $404.87 average price target, shares will climb 12% higher over the one-year timeframe. (See Tesla stock forecast)

data.title: It’s Almost Time for Oracle Stock, Says Investor
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock has had a rough stretch with the shares down by 57% over the past year, even as the business has grown stronger. The company has transformed from a database and software provider into one of the biggest builders of AI infrastructure, and that shift has changed how investors view this name.

However, the big sticking point is the price of that shift. Oracle is spending on data centers at a pace that has pushed free cash flow into negative territory, and the stock has come under pressure as investors question how much capital the AI buildout will eventually swallow.

An investor using the pseudonym Quantryon Capital (QC) understands the concern but believes the selloff overlooks a meaningful shift in how Oracle operates. After the latest quarter, the investor has turned more positive on the stock.

Promotion

Explore ORCZ for 2X short leverage on ORCL

In fiscal Q1 2027 (August quarter), revenue grew 30% year over year to $19.3 billion, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) sales jumped 121% to $7.4 billion. QC’s key point is that the $664 billion backlog is now showing up as revenue. During the quarter, Oracle brought roughly 850 MW of AI capacity and over 300,000 GPUs online, close to triple what it delivered in the previous quarter. Management expects around half of remaining performance obligations to convert into revenue within 36 months. GPU utilization stood at 97.9%, and chips due for renewal were re-leased or resold at a 20% premium to their purchase cost, with most of them over four years old. To QC, this undercuts the fear that fast-aging hardware will lose its value before it pays off.

Beyond infrastructure, QC sees Oracle’s software business as a feeder for OCI. Because Oracle already holds critical enterprise data and workflows, AI gives customers another reason to run those workloads on its cloud. Multicloud database revenue soared 353% in the quarter, and Fusion customers tapped embedded AI over 150 million times.

Spending is still heavy, however. Capital expenditure hit $28 billion in the quarter, and despite record operating cash flow of $23 billion, free cash flow came in at about negative $5 billion. Full-year CapEx is expected at $90 billion to $95 billion. Even so, the investor notes that more than $30 billion in new AI contracts signed during the quarter required no added capital from Oracle, thanks to customer prepayments, customer-owned hardware, and supplier financing. That said, QC stops short of calling the buildout self-funding. Shareholders have already covered part of the bill through dilution, including a $20 billion share sale during the quarter, and the investor wants the next phase of growth to be backed by cash generation rather than more stock sales.

On valuation, QC views a P/E of about 19x as reasonable against FY2027 guidance for at least $90 billion in revenue and $8.10 in non-GAAP EPS. Still, the investor is holding off on a more bullish call until Oracle shows it can keep utilization high, finance the buildout responsibly, and turn its contracted demand into free cash flow without selling more shares.

For now, then, Quantryon Capitalrates the stock a Hold. (To watch Quantryon Capital’s track record, click here)

Five Street analysts are also on the ORCL fence, yet with an additional 27 Buys and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. The average target currently stands at $245.39, implying the stock will gain 85% over the coming months. (See Oracle stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Proof Is on the Way,’ Says Top Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) stock is having another down day as the chip-stock rout drags on. The selloff began at the start of the week, after China’s CXMT unveiled a denser memory chip design aimed at the high-end server market. Hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data and growing fears over debt-fueled AI spending have only added fuel to the fire.

Nevertheless, despite the recent losses, the stock remains one of the market’s standout performers this year, with the shares still up by 378%, riding a NAND flash shortage fueled by AI data center demand.

Against that backdrop, top investor Cavenagh Research remains bullish heading into the company’s October 29 earnings report.

Promotion

Two ETFs to trade SNDK long or short: SNXX & SNDQ

Sandisk’s last quarter (FQ4) was a display of strength. Adjusted EPS of $39.25 came in about 14% above consensus. Data center revenue more than doubled sequentially to $2.98 billion, and edge revenue climbed 48% to $5.43 billion.

Micron’s September report suggests the momentum has held up. Its NAND revenue jumped 42% quarter-over-quarter, helped by prices up roughly 30% and bit shipments up 10%. Micron also expects supply to stay tight through 2028, even with industry output growing in the mid-20% range each year.

Sandisk guided for fiscal Q1 revenue of $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion and EPS of $44 to $46, but it did so before Micron reported. Analysts have since lifted their EPS estimates to about $46. Cavenagh, who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, assumes the growth will slow down, with 40% sequential growth in data center, 15% in edge, and flat consumer sales. Even so, the investor factors in revenue of around $11 billion. Using an 84.5% gross margin and the company’s own guidance for expenses, taxes, and share count, that works out to roughly $48 in EPS.

The 5-star investor thinks the December-quarter outlook will carry more weight than the results themselves. To hit the fiscal 2027 revenue consensus of about $49 billion, Sandisk would need to average roughly $12.7 billion over each of the remaining three quarters. Guidance near $12 billion would keep that path credible. A figure closer to $11 billion would push too much of the load onto the second half.

Looking further ahead, the longer-term story rests on contracts. Sandisk has signed $93.9 billion in total contract value at floor pricing, with an average duration of more than four years. These deals cover about half of fiscal 2027 shipments and two-thirds of fiscal 2028’s, through a mix of fixed prices and variable prices with floors and ceilings. For fiscal 2028 through 2030, management is targeting adjusted gross margins near 80%, operating margins of 75%, and free cash flow margins of 50%. Cavenagh wants to know what Sandisk earns at its contractual floor prices. If gross margins on those sales top 75%, the contracted business would sit close to the company’s long-term target even at the bottom of its price range. Cavenagh says that would justify a higher multiple.

As for valuation, Sandisk trades at about 7x fiscal 2027 consensus earnings, which Cavenagh views as cheap. That view rests on Sandisk sustaining roughly $200 in annual EPS over the long term, which the investor admits is a big ask for a cyclical memory business. Supply outpacing demand, or floor prices that protect volumes more than margins, could undermine that. Still, the contract book already makes the long-term case more credible in Cavenagh’s eyes. More agreements, plus proof of strong margins at the floor, would only strengthen the bull case.

All told, Cavenagh Research rates SNDK stock a Buy. (To watch Cavenagh Research’s track record, click here)

That take sits well with the general Street view. Based on a mix of 15 Buys and 2 Holds, the analyst consensus rates the stock a Strong Buy. Going by the $2,205.59 average price target, a year from now, shares will be changing hands for a 62% premium. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: ‘History Is About to Repeat,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Memory stocks have been put through the wringer this week, with a sector-wide sell-off sparked partly by news of progress at Chinese memory maker CXMT that could make it a tougher rival to the established players. Being one of the segment leaders, Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has been among those hit, with shares sliding by 14% so far this week, as investors worry about what new Chinese competition could mean for memory prices.

Yet, despite the recent losses, the stock is still up by almost 190% year to date and appears to be on a more even keel today (Thursday, Oct. 15). The question now is whether the pullback offers opportunity or whether this is the beginning of a bigger downturn.

At the moment, there appears to be something of a split in how the stock is viewed. Retail investors have been drawn in by Micron’s rapid growth and low earnings multiple, while larger institutions have turned cautious. ARK’s Cathie Wood recently said that although memory demand is trending higher, the industry’s cycles are vicious, and added Chinese supply could make the swings worse.

Promotion

Learn why XOVR invested in Kalshi and the investment thesis behind one of its newest private holdings.

Top investor and Motley Fool contributor Geoffrey Seiler shares that concern, and sees the potential for history to repeat.

Seiler, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, points back to 2000, when Micron set a record high that stood for years. At the time, a memory shortage pushed up chip prices just as PC demand jumped after Y2K, with the internet and the launch of Windows 2000 driving DRAM sales, while phones and other gadgets lifted NAND. Micron’s shares shot up, then collapsed when the dot-com bubble burst, and it took about two decades to climb back. In his view, this year’s rally makes the 2000 run look modest, and the stock only looks cheap if today’s earnings hold.

The investor accepts that some things are different now. AI chips need high-bandwidth memory (HBM), a specialized kind of DRAM, and data centers need huge solid-state drives to store training data. Memory makers are also signing longer-term contracts for the first time, which could smooth out some of the bumps. But Seiler argues HBM isn’t what’s really driving Micron’s results. Because Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix moved so much capacity into HBM, supply of standard DRAM and NAND tightened and prices jumped. He estimates HBM makes up less than 10% of Micron’s sales, leaving it highly exposed to ordinary memory prices. DRAM accounted for 73% of last quarter’s revenue and NAND 26%.

That’s where CXMT matters. The Chinese company has been adding DRAM capacity, taking market share and working on more efficient designs. Its chips are unlikely to be allowed into U.S. data centers, but Seiler says the extra supply alone could be enough to drag conventional prices down.

If that happens, Seiler expects Micron’s stock to fall sharply and not regain its highs, though he doubts it will sink as far as in 2000 and believes the company can stay profitable this time. “Still,” the 5-star investor summed up, “I’d avoid this AI stock for now.” (To watch Seiler’s track record, click here)

That said, Wall Street’s analyst community does not share that view at all. Based on a mix of 27 Buys and 1 Hold, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. At $1,621.67, the average price target suggests shares are undervalued by 77%. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: When the Headline Becomes the Market
data.description:
By: Max Radford

By the time the market understands the story, the damage may already be done. 

For generations, financial markets have operated on a familiar principle: information drives analysis, analysis drives investment decisions, and those decisions determine price. 

Promotion

Explore why XOVR invested in Kalshi and how it identifies innovative private companies before they reach the public markets.

Increasingly, that sequence is running in reverse. 

Today, a headline can move hundreds of billions of dollars in market value before investors have established what the underlying story actually means. Artificial intelligence, automated trading systems, momentum strategies, and an interconnected financial media have created an environment in which the speed of reaction often overwhelms the quality of interpretation. 

More troubling still, the resulting price movement can appear to validate the original headline. 

Two recent episodes in the technology sector illustrate the problem. 

When $70 Billion Becomes $50 Billion 

The first involved reports surrounding OpenAI’s projected revenues. 

A headline suggesting that the company’s expectations had shifted from approximately $70 billion to $50 billion was interpreted as evidence of a serious deterioration in the economics of the artificial intelligence boom. 

If the company at its center was reassessing its financial outlook, investors naturally asked what that meant for the semiconductor manufacturers, cloud providers and technology companies committing unprecedented capital to support it. 

The reaction was immediate. Micron Technology (MU), Oracle (ORCL) and other companies exposed to AI infrastructure spending came under pressure. 

But subsequent discussion of the Financial Times reporting raised a crucial question: were the two figures actually comparable? 

Different reporting periods, accounting treatments and revenue definitions can produce apparently dramatic differences without indicating a deterioration in the underlying business. Forecast revenue, recognized revenue, bookings and annualized run rates are not interchangeable. 

By the time investors examined those distinctions, however, the market had already moved. Algorithms had responded, momentum traders had joined the decline and selling had spread across related companies. Financial media coverage then elevated the market reaction into a global story. 

The headline had helped create the sell-off, and the sell-off appeared to confirm the headline. 

The Chinese Chip Scare 

The sector had barely begun to absorb that episode when another technology story triggered a fresh wave of selling. 

Reports of advances by Chinese semiconductor manufacturer CXMT raised the possibility that China could challenge the technological dominance of established memory chipmakers sooner than expected. The implications appeared significant for companies supplying the global AI infrastructure boom. 

Markets did not wait for that possibility to become commercial reality. 

The selling spread across global semiconductor markets, from Micron Technology in the United States to South Korean giants Samsung Electronics (SSNLF) and SK Hynix (SKHY). The latter were particularly hard hit, with Samsung falling approximately 7.4% and SK Hynix more than 10% in a single session. 

The contagion extended beyond individual companies. South Korea’s semiconductor-heavy KOSPI index plunged approximately 5.5%, demonstrating how the enormous weighting of Samsung and SK Hynix can turn a sector-specific scare into a broader national market sell-off. 

Suddenly, a headline about a potential Chinese technological advance was influencing not only global semiconductor valuations but the direction of an entire national equity market. 

The tail was wagging the dog. Headline-driven selling in a handful of heavyweight stocks was dragging down the wider index, potentially reinforcing further momentum trading, index-related selling and global market anxiety. 

Yet there is a substantial difference between announcing a technological development and delivering a commercially viable product at scale. 

Advanced semiconductor manufacturing requires more than laboratory performance. It depends on production yields, specialized equipment, software compatibility, reliable supply chains, and customers willing to deploy the technology. Those barriers cannot be overcome by a headline alone. 

The Chinese challenge may ultimately prove important. But technological potential and immediate commercial disruption are not the same thing. As several analysts have noted, the threat may currently be closer to a paper tiger than a proven competitive revolution. 

By the time that more measured assessment emerged, the damage had already been done. 

The Feedback Loop 

These episodes matter not simply because markets sometimes overreact. They always have. 

What has changed is the speed and interconnectedness of the reaction. 

AI-powered systems can monitor geopolitical developments, financial publications, earnings announcements, and social media across multiple languages and time zones. Automated strategies can convert that information into trading signals almost instantly. 

Once prices begin to fall, momentum systems may amplify the move. Risk models can trigger further selling, leveraged investors may be forced to reduce positions, and ETF flows or options hedging can transmit pressure across an entire sector. 

The market movement then attracts more media coverage, reinforcing the impression that something fundamental has changed. 

A headline becomes a price movement. The price movement becomes a global news story. The news story encourages another wave of trading. 

By the time deeper analysis arrives, the original narrative may no longer matter. 

How Investors Can Check the Story 

Investors cannot slow the market, but they can slow their own reaction. 

The first step is to locate the original source rather than relying on a headline, social-media post or television summary. Read the full report, identify who is making the claim, and separate confirmed information from estimates, commentary, and speculation. 

The second is to test comparability. When two figures appear to conflict, check whether they refer to the same period, currency, accounting basis, revenue definition and business scope. 

The third is to ask what has actually changed. Has the company revised guidance, lost a customer, reported weaker margins, or disclosed a regulatory problem? Or has the market inferred a threat from an early-stage announcement? 

Finally, examine the price action before acting. A sharp move across an entire sector may reflect momentum trading, ETF flows, forced deleveraging, or options hedging rather than a fresh change in fundamental value. That does not make the move irrelevant, but it does mean it should not automatically be chased. 

Algorithms or Fundamentals? 

This is the central challenge for modern investors. 

Traditional valuation models depend on earnings, cash flows, competitive positioning, and long-term growth expectations. None of those necessarily changes because an alarming headline appears on a trading terminal. Yet the market price can change dramatically within minutes. 

For short-term traders, understanding momentum, liquidity, and automated market behavior may be essential. For long-term investors, the opportunity may lie in identifying moments when prices have become detached from underlying value. 

The difficulty is knowing which is happening before the next wave of selling arrives. 

In today’s markets, algorithms may determine the price in the short term. But fundamentals must ultimately determine the value. 

The uncomfortable question is how much damage can be done in the time between the two.

data.title: ‘Watch Out for the Trap,’ Says Top Investor About CoreWeave Stock
data.description:
Jim Cramer did it again. Just hours after the Mad Money host praised CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) as the only AI neocloud in its class he trusts, the stock tumbled about 15% on Wednesday, and the weakness has continued in Thursday’s session, with the stock down by 8% as of writing. On social media, Cramer’s picks are often treated as a signal to do the opposite, and this one will only add to the joke. To be fair, though, his endorsement wasn’t the reason for the slide. The drop came from new worries about how much the company owes.

CoreWeave rents Nvidia-powered GPU servers to AI developers who would rather not spend years and billions building their own data centers. Demand is clearly there. Microsoft, OpenAI and Meta are all customers, and the company ended Q2 with a revenue backlog of about $104 billion.

Top investor Adam Spatacco, who contributes to The Motley Fool, thinks that backlog tells only half the story. In his view, landing big contracts is one thing, but generating enough cash to pay for the hardware behind them is quite another.

Promotion

Double your CRWV exposure with Tradr's CWVX

The selloff followed an essay by billionaire venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya. He pointed out that CoreWeave’s $1.25 billion bond tranche due in 2032 briefly traded at a 15% yield, compared with the 9.6% it carried when issued in June. Yields rise as bond prices fall, so the jump shows debt investors are getting nervous about being repaid.

The numbers can explain why. CoreWeave carried roughly $35.1 billion of debt at the end of Q2, or close to $51.6 billion once operating and financing leases are included. In the first half of 2026, it brought in about $3.7 billion of operating cash flow. That fell well short of the $6.2 billion it owed in principal and interest over the same period.

Meanwhile, the outlook doesn’t look great either. Visible Alpha consensus figures point to negative free cash flow of $25 billion this year, $28 billion in 2027 and $18 billion in 2028. CoreWeave will therefore keep relying on outside money, including private credit, until its data centers mature and start producing cash.

The investor sees a timing mismatch at the heart of the problem. The spending happens up front, while the revenue arrives gradually over years. If AI demand stays hot, the bet could pay off handsomely. But a slowdown in AI budgets, delayed customer rollouts or newer Nvidia chips that make older hardware less valuable could leave CoreWeave paying hefty interest on less profitable assets.

While the market evidently got concerned about CoreWeave’s financial situation, Spatacco, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, stresses that bankruptcy isn’t necessarily a given. Still, with rates rising and years of cash burn forecast, he won’t be buying the dip. “Chasing the downward spiral could turn out to be a trap, catching a falling knife,” the 5-star investor summed up. “I consider CoreWeave too speculative for most long-term investors and would prefer to see improving unit economics and a healthier balance sheet before buying.” (To watch Spatacco’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘Stay Cool,’ Says Analyst About Rocket Lab Stock
data.description:
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) investors were already a pretty depressed bunch before today, given the stock’s massive pullback from its May high, but Thursday’s action has made Wednesday’s closing price rather appealing.

The stock is being subjected to a heavy beating in today’s session, down by 13% as of writing, after the company announced the one thing investors did not want to hear: a debut launch delay for its Neutron rocket.

In a post-market update on Wednesday, Rocket Lab said Neutron’s maiden launch has been pushed back to 2027, having previously been targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. The cause was a set of manufacturing flaws found in the propellant domes of the rocket’s first stage. The company says the problem has been fixed, but identifying the root cause and overhauling its production methods took long enough to knock the schedule back.

Promotion

55% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks
Learn more about TipRanks Premium

In January, a stage one tank burst during testing. Rocket Lab responded by bringing production of that tank in-house, aiming to gain efficiencies from its new automated fiber placement (AFP) machine. The original tank had been built by an outside supplier using hand-laid composite. At the same time, the company redesigned the structure to remove joints and add extra carbon composite thickness in certain sections. Those thicker sections later turned out to contain voids, which triggered an investigation and a revamp of the manufacturing process. Rocket Lab has since built a new aft dome and verified that the fix works, which gave it the green light to begin work on a replacement forward dome, now in progress. The result is that Neutron’s debut is now slated for no earlier than 2027.

As for what comes next, the company plans to fabricate, cure, analyze and test the new forward dome before the first quarter, with both domes expected to be joined into a complete first stage during Q1. After that, the rocket must clear a hydrostatic test, then a cryogenic test, and finally a full-stack test on the launch pad before it can fly.

So, following the disappointment, what should investors do with the stock now? Well, calm down a bit, appears to be KeyBanc analyst Michael Leshock’s stance. The analyst is not entirely surprised by this development. “We believe the delay was largely anticipated given management’s recent commentary, acknowledging that the window for a year-end launch was narrowing, and emphasizing the importance of balancing Neutron’s timeline with the ability to scale future production and launch cadence.”

Leshock now sees the second quarter of 2027 as a “reasonable timeline” for the first flight, while noting that a first-quarter launch is “not off the table upon execution.”

The analyst has left his 2026 forecasts untouched, as Neutron’s inaugural flight was never expected to bring in revenue. For 2027, however, he has trimmed his revenue estimate by roughly $53 million to account for one fewer paying Neutron mission that year. His projections for the Space Systems segment stay the same, as Leshock continues to expect robust growth there and regards Rocket Lab as a “top beneficiary of the fast-growing space ecosystem.”

“We believe the market sell-off presents a meaningful opportunity for growth-orientated, LT investors, as the LT story remains intact. We continue to view RKLB as a leader within the space sector and believe Neutron will achieve a commanding share of the medium-lift launch market over the coming years,” Leshock summed up.

That said, while Leshock maintained a Buy rating on the shares, he lowered his price target from $135 to $100 to “reflect the updated Neutron timeline and broader multiple compression across high-growth space equities.” Still, there’s potential upside of 96% from current levels. data.title: Broadcom vs. Marvell: One AI Stock Is for Buying, One Is for Taking Profits, Says Investor
data.description:
In the real world, Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Marvell (NASDAQ:MRVL) have spent 2026 riding the same wave. Both design custom silicon for the hyperscalers racing to build out AI data centers, and both recently delivered strong quarters on the back of that demand. Yet their shares have gone in opposite directions. Despite a recent pullback, Marvell shares are up by 174% this year, while Broadcom, by far the larger company with a market cap near $1.9 trillion, has now actually delivered modest losses.

That split comes as investors grow pickier about which AI winners still have room to run. Big spending plans from the cloud giants remain intact, but the market is now paying closer attention to valuations, funding risks, and how durable each company’s place in the supply chain really is.

An investor using the pseudonym The Alpha Analyst (AA) has been digging into exactly that question. In the investor’s view, the two businesses are almost mirror images. They sell into the same group of customers, depend on the same capex budgets, and wrestle with the same supply chain constraints. Both are even seeing margins diluted as custom work grows as a share of sales. Earnings growth over the next couple of years also looks broadly similar. So what explains the gap? According to AA, it comes down almost entirely to valuation.

Promotion

Technology investors who refuse to pick growth or income now have TDAQ.

To compare like with like, AA lines up Broadcom’s fiscal 2028 against Marvell’s fiscal 2029, since the two companies’ financial years end three months apart. Even that far out, Marvell trades at close to twice Broadcom’s earnings multiple, with Broadcom sitting at around 11.4x projected earnings. The investor doesn’t think the slight difference in growth comes close to justifying that premium.

AA does give Marvell some credit. The company has a habit of setting ambitious targets, then lifting them and hitting them ahead of time. Its data center goal has been raised more than once and is now expected a year early, while its fiscal 2028 revenue outlook jumped from around $18 billion to roughly $20 billion in just a few weeks. With scale-up optics as another possible catalyst, Marvell has plenty of ways to keep surprising.

Broadcom is the quieter story. Management has laid out roughly $115 billion in AI chip revenue for fiscal 2027 and about $230 billion for fiscal 2028, says supply is secured for both, and doesn’t plan to revisit those numbers every quarter. That means fewer fireworks, but also a far more predictable path.

Each company carries its own risk, but AA sees them as very different in nature. For Broadcom, the concern is concentration. Anthropic is set to become its biggest custom chip customer next year, with OpenAI following by 2028, and Broadcom is even helping to finance their buildouts. If either lab struggles to pay on time, part of that $230 billion target could slip. The investor expects Anthropic to stay on schedule and some of OpenAI’s 2028 orders to be pushed back, but views this as a timing issue rather than a broken thesis, especially given the cushion provided by a low multiple.

Marvell’s risk, as AA sees it, is more fundamental. Much of its recent target upgrade comes from smaller chips that sit next to the accelerator, rather than the accelerator itself. These parts are easier for rivals to replace. Broadcom faces competition from MediaTek at Google, but there a second supplier dents market share without ending the relationship. For Marvell, losing an attach socket could mean losing the customer altogether.

The scales are tipped further when taking earnings quality into account. Broadcom’s non-GAAP operating margin stands near 68%, compared with about 37% at Marvell, where stock-based compensation has climbed to nearly 12% of revenue from under 8% a year earlier.

Putting it all together, AA rates Broadcom a Buy as a steady stock to build over time, and Marvell a Hold. Those sitting on big Marvell gains may want to take some money off the table and wait for either a bigger pullback or fresh accelerator wins before stepping back in. (To watch The Alpha Analyst’s track record, click here)

The Street, however, sees no reason to choose between the pair. Both claim Strong Buy consensus ratings and are projected to deliver strong returns over the following months. AVGO’s $519.21 average price target points to one-year gains of 50%. Meanwhile, MRVL’s $354.56 average target offers 12-month upside of 44.5%. (See AVGO stock forecast or MRVL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘There’s Not a Good Enough Reason,’ Says Top Investor About SpaceX Stock
data.description:
Whatever you might think of Elon Musk, you can’t accuse him of lacking ambition. His latest move marks another bold expansion for SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), which is looking to move beyond satellite internet and enter the mobile carrier market, potentially unlocking a substantial new revenue stream. Its growing spectrum portfolio, Starlink network, and existing customer base could give it a competitive edge. However, building a mobile business is far more complex than providing satellite broadband, raising questions about the capital required, execution risks, and potential profitability of the expansion.

Of course, as is often the case with Musk, there’s hype involved with any new move. With this in mind, 5-star investor Dhierin Bechai remains bullish on SpaceX but is skeptical about its mobile ambitions. The investor believes the company risks spreading itself too thin, drawing comparisons with Tesla’s strategy of pursuing multiple ambitious ventures while profitability comes under pressure.

Bechai points to SpaceX’s spectrum agreements, including $19.6 billion in announced consideration for EchoStar licenses and a reported $8 billion deal for Grain Management’s 800 MHz portfolio. These acquisitions provide valuable transmission rights, but SpaceX still needs sufficient ground infrastructure, network capacity, and compatible devices. Management expects next-generation Starlink Mobile satellites to begin launching in 2027, although meaningful revenue contributions could take until 2028, with substantial competitive pressure on established carriers potentially taking several more years.

Promotion

High conviction on SPCX? Try Tradr's SPCM or SPCG

The investor sees opportunities for AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile to lose pricing power before suffering significant subscriber losses. SpaceX could attract existing Starlink customers with bundled internet and mobile services, particularly in rural areas. However, established carriers retain an advantage in densely populated areas, where dependable indoor coverage and network capacity are essential. Incumbents are also developing satellite connectivity alternatives, potentially reducing their reliance on Starlink.

Bechai’s central concern is that SpaceX might underestimate the cost and complexity of building a competitive terrestrial network. Satellite connectivity works well where conventional coverage is limited, but that does not mean it can match established carriers on price or performance in well-served markets. Small cellular base stations and femtocells have limited coverage areas, meaning broader adoption would require substantial additional infrastructure, acquisitions, or regulatory authorization for expanded direct-to-cell services.

The investor also warns that simultaneous investments in Starship, AI infrastructure, and mobile connectivity could delay cash generation. Although higher EBITDA expectations support the broader investment case, capital expenditures are rising, and free cash flow is expected to remain deeply negative as infrastructure spending continues.

Ultimately, however, Bechai, who ranks among the top 5% of investors on TipRanks, keeps a bullish stance on SpaceX because of its broader growth prospects, not its mobile expansion. The investor sees potential in serving existing Starlink customers but doubts the company can become a major mobile carrier without considerable additional investment. The big question is whether the opportunity justifies the capital required to compete with established networks.

All told, Bechai maintained a Buy rating on the shares. (To watch Bechai’s track record, click here)

data.title: ‘You Better Run,’ Says Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) shares have been feeling the pressure this week after Chinese memory-chip maker ChangXin Memory Technologies reportedly made progress on a new DRAM architecture that could increase memory density and intensify competition. The development has raised concerns that Chinese manufacturers could pose a greater competitive threat to established players, potentially putting pressure on the pricing power that has helped drive Micron’s earnings growth.

The sell-off also reflects mounting doubts about the sustainability of the AI-driven memory boom. Weakness in South Korean equities, which have helped lead the sector’s rally, and questions about AI spending following reports of a revenue shortfall at OpenAI have further weighed on sentiment.

Still, Micron’s recent quarterly results were nothing less than spectacular, so is the latest scare just another example of the market getting all worked up over nothing?

Promotion

Learn why XOVR invested in Kalshi and the investment thesis behind one of its newest private holdings.

Not at all, says investor Kevin George, who argues that it’s time to seriously consider the risks of a changing competitive landscape.

George argues that memory manufacturers could be approaching a familiar boom-and-bust cycle. Micron’s fiscal 2026 results were outstanding, and management expects even stronger performance in fiscal 2027, with supply and demand conditions remaining tight into 2028. However, DRAM accounted for 76% of Micron’s earnings in fiscal 2026, while sales volumes rose by only a mid-single-digit percentage. This suggests that higher prices, rather than substantial production growth, have driven much of the company’s financial improvement. If Chinese manufacturers add meaningful capacity, pricing power could weaken.

Warnings from prominent industry figures reinforce these concerns. Cathie Wood has cautioned that additional Chinese competitors could intensify the memory market’s notoriously volatile cycles. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan has also questioned whether investors fully understand the risks surrounding AI-related investments, particularly when major AI businesses continue to spend heavily on training without establishing sustainable profitability.

Micron’s financial position nevertheless remains strong. In the latest quarter, revenue climbed from $11.3 billion to $54.2 billion year over year, while cash and marketable investments increased from $11.94 billion to $73.48 billion. Long-term customer agreements also offer some reassurance, with Micron adding 10 strategic customer agreements and securing commitments extending beyond 2030 in certain cases. However, these agreements have yet to be tested during a significant industry downturn.

Interestingly, while Micron’s forward P/E ratio of around 5.4x suggests the stock is inexpensive relative to expected earnings, George believes investors could be underestimating the risks to those earnings. With the stock trading at 8.37x sales, 128% above the sector average and 58% higher than its five-year average, its valuation could come under pressure if Chinese competition increases supply and weakens memory prices. Although it might take one to two years to materially affect market share, investors could begin pricing in that risk sooner. Combined with fragile Korean market sentiment and uncertainty surrounding AI spending, for George, the threat to Micron outweighs its near-term earnings strength.

Accordingly, George rates the stock a Sell. (To watch George’s track record, click here)

data.title: Intuit vs. Oracle: One Software Stock Faces Competition, the Other Is a Risk Worth Taking, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Intuit (NASDAQ:INTU) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) are established technology companies with very different growth opportunities. Intuit makes financial software for consumers and small businesses, with TurboTax and QuickBooks helping millions of people manage taxes, bookkeeping and other financial tasks. Oracle, meanwhile, supplies cloud infrastructure and enterprise software to large organizations, positioning itself to benefit from growing demand for computing power and artificial intelligence (AI).

Both stocks have taken a hammering over the past year, each shedding more than 50%, but their businesses generate substantial profits and benefit from recurring customer relationships. However, their investment cases are diverging. Intuit must defend its established position against cheaper alternatives and emerging AI tools, while Oracle is investing heavily in cloud infrastructure to capture demand from businesses building and deploying AI applications. The key question is whether Intuit’s established business offers better value or whether Oracle’s expansion provides greater long-term potential.

Top investor John Ballard, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, has been assessing these differences when mulling over which stock offers the more compelling long-term opportunity.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

Looking at Intuit, the company generated $21 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026, an increase of around 14% year over year. Net income approached $4.6 billion, while free cash flow reached $8.6 billion. These figures demonstrate the company’s ability to turn its software subscriptions and financial services into substantial profits and cash generation.

Its financial position also looks relatively conservative. A debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.4 times indicates relatively low leverage, while a current ratio of around 1.5 times suggests reasonable short-term financial flexibility.

However, Ballard sees growing competitive pressure as a significant concern. Intuit faces rival tax-preparation services, fintech companies and potentially government-backed tax-filing initiatives. AI could make financial tools cheaper and easier to develop, putting pressure on the company’s ability to charge premium prices. Although QuickBooks and more complicated tax services may prove harder to replace, the investor questions whether Intuit can maintain its hold on individual taxpayers over the next decade.

Oracle generated approximately $67 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue, up 17% year over year, while net income reached roughly $17 billion. Its central growth opportunity is Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, which provides the computing capacity needed to run demanding business applications and AI workloads.

Ballard points to Oracle’s substantial contracted cloud backlog as evidence of strong demand. Recent quarterly revenue growth accelerated to 30% year over year as the company worked to fulfil customer commitments.

The challenge is funding that expansion. Oracle is building data centers and acquiring the infrastructure needed to meet demand, leaving it with considerably more debt than Intuit. Its debt-to-equity ratio stood at approximately 2.3 times in August 2026. Furthermore, free cash flow was negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, as capital expenditure reached $55.7 billion. Delays in construction, chip shortages or weaker cloud demand could therefore create problems.

Nevertheless, Ballard believes Oracle’s cash generation offers some reassurance. Operating cash flow reached almost $47 billion on a trailing-12-month basis, helping fund data center investments without relying entirely on additional borrowing. Its debt-to-equity ratio also declined from 3.6 times at the end of May to 2.3 times in August, suggesting its leverage position had improved.

Valuation adds another dimension to the comparison. Intuit trades at approximately 12.6 times forward earnings and 3.8 times sales, compared with Oracle at around 16.8 times forward earnings and 6.1 times sales. These multiples suggest Intuit is cheaper, but a lower valuation does not necessarily mean a stock is undervalued if competition threatens future growth.

Ballard acknowledges that Oracle’s volatile share price and infrastructure spending make it a riskier investment. Still, the investor favours its exposure to the expanding AI ecosystem over Intuit’s uncertain competitive position. “I would rather invest in the company building the future than in the one that could be vulnerable to moat erosion from competition,” the 5-star investor summed up. Memory stocks Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and SK hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) have been having a bit of a meltdown this week, enduring an ongoing sell-off after Chinese chipmaker CXMT revealed plans to introduce a next-generation DDR5 memory product featuring 4F² architecture and hybrid bonding by the end of the year. The announcement has raised concerns that China could become a more serious competitor in the DRAM market, threatening the pricing power and profitability of established manufacturers.

However, Rosenblatt’s Kevin Cassidy, who ranks among the top 1% of Street stock experts, sees the market’s reaction as “overblown,” arguing that investors are exaggerating the immediate competitive threat. He believes the market might be overlooking the technical challenges involved in bringing new memory architectures to mass production, as well as the changing nature of demand driven by artificial intelligence.

The analyst says that introducing a more compact memory design does not automatically translate into lower manufacturing costs or commercial success.

Promotion

Curious why XOVR invested in Kalshi? Explore the long-term strategy behind the investment.

Cassidy notes that the DRAM industry has spent roughly two decades refining the established 6F² architecture, gradually improving density through successive manufacturing generations. Although leading manufacturers are exploring the more compact 4F² design, the economics remain challenging until production technology advances beyond the current leading edge. Assuming CXMT uses a manufacturing process around 17nm, compared with approximately 12nm for industry leaders, Cassidy estimates that its 4F² memory cells could still occupy about 34% more space than competitors’ 6F² cells. This undermines the assumption that the new architecture automatically delivers a cost advantage.

Cassidy also points out that CXMT has not disclosed manufacturing yields or production volumes. Developing a prototype is one thing; producing reliable chips at competitive costs and on a large scale is another. Until more details emerge, the planned launch offers limited evidence that CXMT can challenge established suppliers commercially.

Beyond the technological questions, Cassidy argues that AI is fundamentally changing the DRAM market. Historically, memory manufacturers endured recurring oversupply, falling prices and periods of financial losses. Demand from PC and smartphone manufacturers was highly sensitive to pricing, while short planning cycles made it difficult to anticipate inventory swings.

AI infrastructure has changed that, however. Memory capacity, bandwidth and availability have become ever more important to system performance, while hyperscalers and cloud providers typically plan their infrastructure investments years ahead. Cassidy believes this offers greater demand visibility than traditional consumer electronics markets.

Cassidy also highlights the high cost and long lead times involved in expanding DRAM production. New fabrication plants can take three to five years to become operational and cost more than $10 billion, making it essential for manufacturers to have clear evidence of future demand before committing to additional capacity. In his view, this favors a more disciplined investment approach rather than building new facilities on the assumption that demand will eventually materialize.

Finally, the analyst believes memory stock valuations fail to reflect these changing industry dynamics. Stocks in the sector trade at roughly five to seven times earnings, suggesting investors continue to price in the traditional boom-and-bust cycle. “We believe the market is assigning too much weight to CXMT’s architectural announcement and less to incumbent manufacturers’ execution and the visibility by AI spending,” the 5-star analyst summed up.

Accordingly, Cassidy reiterated a Buy rating on Micron, backed by a $1,900 price target, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 99%. At the same time, Cassidy maintained a Buy rating on SK Hynix, with a $320 price target suggesting shares will gain 104% in the months ahead. (To watch Cassidy’s track record, click here)

Both these stocks get overwhelmingly positive support elsewhere on the Street, the pair claiming Strong Buy consensus ratings. MU’s average price target stands at $1,621.67, implying the stock will climb 70% over the one-year timeframe. SKHY stock is expected to gain 62%, given the average target clocks in at $254.70. data.title: ‘If Not Now, Then When?’ Says Top Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has been going all in on AI infrastructure, investing heavily to capitalize on surging demand for cloud computing. The strategy is delivering impressive sales growth, with cloud revenue accelerating and customer commitments reaching $664 billion.

However, the expansion comes at a steep cost, with rising capital expenditures, negative free cash flow, and mounting debt raising questions about the company’s ability to turn its AI investments into lasting profits.

With the stock down by 55% over the past year, the valuation reflects these concerns, but continued demand for AI infrastructure could provide a path to recovery. 5-star investor Johnny Zhang believes Oracle offers an attractive opportunity, arguing that its growth prospects outweigh the financial risks as long as customers continue to follow through on their commitments.

Promotion

High conviction ORCL bears now have this Tradr ETF

That specifically pertains to OpenAI, Oracle’s largest customer. OpenAI reportedly expects to generate $70 billion in revenue in 2026, potentially strengthening its ability to meet its $300 billion agreement with Oracle. That deal accounts for a substantial portion of Oracle’s RPO (remaining performance obligations), or contracted revenue yet to be recognized. Zhang believes the infrastructure spending required to fulfill these commitments should eventually translate into stronger sales and attractive returns.

Oracle’s revenue growth accelerated to nearly 30% year over year in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, while cloud revenue jumped 61.5%. Management expects cloud revenue growth to reach 67% in the second quarter. Although RPO growth slowed to 45.8% from more than 300% in fiscal 2026, Zhang argues that such a slowdown was inevitable after an exceptional period of expansion. The subsequent decline in bookings also reflects a tougher comparison with the previous year.

Nevertheless, profitability remains a challenge. Adj. gross margin fell to 61% from 68.7% a year ago as lower-margin infrastructure services expanded, while interest expenses reached $5.1 billion over the trailing 12 months. Still, Zhang considers Oracle’s debt manageable, pointing to interest coverage of 5.71 times and net debt of 2.12 times adjusted EBITDA.

Cash flow is a bigger concern. Oracle expects to spend $90 billion to $95 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2027, while free cash flow has been negative for six consecutive quarters, reaching a $28.7 billion deficit over the trailing 12 months.

Nevertheless, Zhang believes the market has already priced in substantial risks. Oracle’s forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 17.3 times from 20 times four months earlier. The biggest threat is a slowdown in AI spending, particularly if OpenAI falls short of expectations. That could leave Oracle with expensive infrastructure, weaker cash flow, and greater credit risk. “That’s why the stock trades at a cheap multiple,” the investor summed up, “so I believe the risk and reward remain attractive.”

Accordingly, Zhang rates ORCL stock a Buy. (To watch Zhang’s track record, click here)

Most Street analysts are thinking along the same lines. Based on a mix of 27 Buys, 5 Holds and 1 Sell, the stock receives a Strong Buy consensus rating. Over the next 12 months, the shares are expected to appreciate by 72%, given the average price target clocks in at $245.39. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Another Tall Tale,’ Says Top Investor About SpaceX Stock
data.description:
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) has built its reputation on revolutionising the space industry, with its reusable rockets and Starlink satellite network creating new opportunities in global connectivity. Now, the company is looking to expand beyond satellite internet and challenge established telecommunications providers through Starlink Mobile. Its latest move, an approximately $8 billion acquisition of low-band wireless spectrum, signals an ambitious push into the US mobile market. However, the deal has also raised concerns about whether satellite technology can compete with traditional cellular networks, particularly in densely populated cities where reliable coverage and network capacity are essential.

The acquisition comes as SpaceX pursues its costly AI ambitions, adding another major investment to an already capital-intensive business. While the company has substantial financial resources and significant growth opportunities, its increasingly ambitious plans raise questions about capital allocation and whether its valuation adequately reflects the risks involved.

For top investor Julia Ostian, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, argues that the acquisition does little to address the company’s fundamental challenges.

Promotion

High conviction on SPCX? Try Tradr's SPCM or SPCG

Ostian believes SpaceX is paying a premium to enter an intensely competitive industry with limited growth prospects. The company agreed to acquire low-band spectrum licenses for approximately $8 billion, adding to the roughly $17 billion it committed to acquiring mid-band spectrum from EchoStar. Although the new licenses could improve indoor reception, Ostian argues that spectrum alone cannot replicate the extensive infrastructure built by established wireless operators over decades.

Low-band frequencies travel farther and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher frequencies, but the spectrum SpaceX acquired remains limited. Ostian estimates that its allocation amounts to roughly one-third of the low-band spectrum held by major competitors. Furthermore, satellites orbit hundreds of kilometres above the Earth, making reliable indoor connectivity considerably more difficult than with conventional cell towers.

Capacity presents another obstacle. Ostian’s calculations suggest that a satellite beam using the acquired spectrum could deliver approximately 7–14 megabits per second across a vast geographical area, potentially serving millions of people. That would make competing with terrestrial networks in densely populated cities particularly challenging. SpaceX may therefore need substantial ground infrastructure to deliver a genuinely competitive service, undermining the cost advantages of its satellite-based approach.

The financial implications are equally concerning. SpaceX can afford the acquisition, having held approximately $93.5 billion in cash at the end of the second quarter. However, Ostian highlights the company’s enormous capital expenditure requirements, particularly its AI ambitions. SpaceX spent $18.4 billion on capital expenditure in the quarter, including $15.8 billion directed towards AI. Additional borrowing to finance AI infrastructure could intensify competition for capital within the business.

Ostian also questions the strategic rationale behind entering wireless telecommunications. With Starlink’s average revenue per user declining from $85 to $66, the investor suspects SpaceX needs fresh growth narratives to sustain investor enthusiasm. The wireless market offers an appealing story, but Ostian disputes management’s suggestion that its annual revenue opportunity approaches $600 billion, citing industry estimates closer to $220 billion.

Then there’s the famously exorbitant valuation. At approximately $2.12 trillion, SpaceX trades at 35 times Ostian’s projected 2027 revenue of $60 billion. Even using a more optimistic $100 billion revenue forecast, the multiple remains around 21 times sales. Ostian considers such a valuation excessive for a capital-intensive business facing substantial execution risks. “Summarizing it all,” the 5-star investor summed up, “it’s a nice little story that I refuse to believe in.”

As such, Ostian maintained a Strong Sell rating on the stock, arguing that the spectrum acquisition does not meaningfully improve SpaceX’s competitive position enough to justify its premium valuation. (To watch Ostian’s track record, click here)

Two Street analysts agree with Ostian’s bearish thesis, but with an additional 28 Buys and 5 Holds, the stock receives a Moderate Buy consensus rating. At $216.00, the average price target implies shares will gain 37.5% in the months ahead. (See SpaceX stock forecast)
